articles.title: Export via Email
articles.author: Jnanendra Avinash Golakoti
articles.content:
[html]
Exports & Reports · Automated Report Delivery

Export via Email

What Is Export via Email?
An automated report delivery mechanism combining two capabilities: Export (generating a structured CSV file from a worksheet) and Email Delivery (attaching the generated file and sending it to stakeholders automatically). The feature eliminates manual download-attach-send cycles entirely.
Section 01
How It Works — Three-Stage Pipeline
Sequential Stages
  1. Manual Trigger (or embedded step) — authorized user triggers the process, or the export fires automatically as a step within a larger parent workflow (e.g. month-end close, payroll pipeline)
  2. Run Export — CSV Generation — connects to the designated worksheet, applies the pre-configured date range filter, and exports as a CSV (or multiple worksheets bundled as a ZIP archive)
  3. Send Email — Dispatch — retrieves the generated file using its internal reference, attaches it automatically, addresses to recipient, and sends with a consistent subject line
File Integrity
Because the file reference is passed directly between stages, there is no risk of attaching the wrong file or an outdated version. The attachment always reflects exactly what was generated in the current run.
Section 02
Key Components
Component Roles
ComponentRole
Manual TriggerInitiates the pipeline; all parameters pre-configured in the workflow definition
Export EngineQueries the worksheet, applies parameters, produces CSV or ZIP output
Email ServiceComposes and dispatches the report email — supports CC, BCC, custom subjects, delivery logging
File Attachment HandlerBridges the export engine and email service — passes file identifier to prevent duplication
Section 03
Configuration Options
  • Date & Time — custom period selection, preset periods (this week, this month, last quarter, year-to-date), fiscal year alignment
  • Output Format — CSV (single worksheet) or ZIP archive (multiple worksheets)
  • Currency Conversion — specify output currency for multi-region exports
  • Email — pre-configured recipients, CC/BCC support, custom subject and body templates
  • Scheduled Delivery — can be embedded in a scheduled workflow for daily, weekly, or monthly cadence
Section 04
Best Practices
  • Always validate recipient email addresses before saving the workflow configuration
  • Use descriptive subject lines including the report name and date range for easy archiving
  • Test the workflow end-to-end with a sandbox email before deploying to production recipients
  • Keep email body content brief — the attachment is the deliverable; the email is just the wrapper
  • For scheduled reports, align delivery time with the recipient's start-of-day
  • Exports can only be generated from a Worksheet — the source must be a configured worksheet in the platform

articles.title: Scheduled Report Delivery
articles.author: Dharma Teja Taddi
articles.content:
[html]
Exports & Reports · Automation Guide

Scheduled Report Delivery

What Is Scheduled Report Delivery?
A core automation capability that generates and distributes reports to recipients automatically at predefined intervals — with zero manual intervention after initial configuration. Once activated, the workflow runs independently: queries the workbook, generates the output file, and dispatches it via email on schedule.
Section 01
Prerequisites
Required Before Configuring
  • Dataset — containing the data to be exported, up to date with all required fields, dimensions, and measures
  • Workbook — the dataset must be imported into a Workbook, which is the data source for the export action
  • Export Configuration — an Export must be created from the workbook before configuring the workflow, defining output format, sheet selection, filters, and currency settings
Section 02
Three-Node Workflow Pipeline
Sequential Execution
  1. Trigger Node — defines the schedule (standard frequency or cron expression) with execution time, timezone, and exclusion dates
  2. Run Export Excel — connects to the configured workbook, applies filters, and generates the output file (CSV for single worksheet; ZIP for multiple)
  3. Send Email — attaches the generated file using the dynamic file_id variable from the export node and dispatches to configured recipients
Section 03
Scheduling Options
Two Scheduling Methods
OptionMethodBest For
Standard SchedulePredefined frequency options — daily, weekly, monthlyCommon delivery cadences
Cron ScheduleCustom cron expression in the Schedule fieldAdvanced scheduling standard frequencies cannot cover
Section 04
Export Capabilities
Additional Capabilities
  • Currency Type — specify output currency for multi-region reports
  • Row-level filters — scope exported rows to an authorized data subset
  • Statements and Metrics — include KPI snapshots alongside worksheet data
  • Multiple worksheets — each exported as a separate CSV and bundled into a single ZIP archive
Section 05
Activation Checklist
Go-Live Steps
  1. Import the required dataset into a workbook in Bluecopa
  2. Create an export using that workbook, defining output format and sheet selection
  3. Configure a Trigger node with the required schedule (standard or cron)
  4. Set execution time, timezone, and any exclusion dates
  5. Add the Run Export Excel action with export ID and input settings
  6. Add the Send Email action, referencing the export node's file_id as the attachment
  7. Configure recipient addresses, subject line, and email body
  8. Activate the workflow to enable automated recurring delivery
Section 06
Scheduling Best Practices
  • Align delivery time with the recipient's start-of-day so reports are ready when work begins
  • Use the Exclude Schedule field to suppress delivery on public holidays and non-business days
  • For time-sensitive reports, use Cron scheduling for precise minute-level control
  • Always configure timezone explicitly — never rely on server defaults
  • Use a clear subject line including report name and time period: e.g. Collections Report — June 2026
  • Restrict recipients to those who require the data — avoid broad distribution lists

articles.title: REST API Connector
articles.author: Sai Kumar
articles.content:
[html]
Connectors & Integrations · Technical Configuration Guide

REST API Connector

What Is the REST API Connector?
The dedicated network transport infrastructure layer within Bluecopa. It encapsulates HTTP/HTTPS protocol mechanics, manages connection pools, builds URL strings, handles low-level serialization, and manages secure communication pathways. It is completely agnostic to business logic — its sole purpose is safe, efficient data transmission.
Section 01
Two-Phase Configuration Framework

Setting up a REST API Connector involves a rigid two-step framework managed under Main Menu → Data → External Data.

Configuration Phases
PhaseNamePurpose
AConnection Profile (The Gateway)Establishes the root network parameters for communicating with a third-party host
BAPI Action Definition (The Endpoint)Declares individual operational endpoints as API Actions on the verified gateway
Section 02
Phase A — Connection Profile Configuration
Configuration Fields
  • Connection Name & Description — unique identifier for the gateway (e.g. SampleHTTPConnection)
  • Connection Specification — select HTTP for standard REST integrations (SQL, BigQuery, BlueDB also supported)
  • Base URL — root network location for the API endpoint (e.g. https://mockapi.randomserver.com)
  • Authentication Strategy — NoAuth for public APIs; Basic Auth, API Key, Bearer Token, or OAuth for protected endpoints
  • Timeout — maximum seconds to wait for server response (default: 30 seconds)
  • SSL Validation — enforce HTTPS to encrypt all payload data in transit
  • Test Connection — click Save then Test to verify socket accessibility before adding API Actions
Section 03
Phase B — API Action Definition
Action Configuration
  • Action Name & Description — distinct identifier for each endpoint (e.g. Retrieve Order Details)
  • HTTP Verb — GET (retrieve), POST (create), PUT (overwrite), DELETE (remove), PATCH (partial update)
  • Endpoint Path with Jinja — trailing path relative to Base URL with dynamic field markers (e.g. v1/api/orders/{order_id})
  • Template Parameters — dynamic fields calculated at runtime (e.g. {order_id} mapped to actual order ID)
  • Request Body — for POST/PUT/PATCH, provide the request body template in raw JSON format
Section 04
Security & Governance Best Practices
  • Secret Isolation — never hardcode passwords or client secrets in workflow canvas parameters. Use the platform's encrypted secret vault.
  • Egress Protocols — enforce HTTPS/TLS across all connectors to prevent payload interception
  • Throttling Compliance — configure endpoints to handle 429 rate-limit codes gracefully to prevent remote server blocks
Section 05
REST Connector vs API Integration Node
Architectural Distinction
DimensionREST API ConnectorAPI Integration Node
LayerInfrastructure — transport protocolBusiness process — orchestration logic
Configured inExternal Data > Settings panelWorkflow Canvas
HandlesNetwork sockets, TLS, JSON serializationData mapping, state tracking, retry loops
Failure handlingTransient TCP/socket dropsConditional branches, fallback paths
User personaIntegration Engineer / Platform OwnerWorkflow Developer / Solution Architect

articles.title: Monitoring & Alerting — Pipeline Troubleshooting
articles.author: Bhuvaneshwari Jangam
articles.content:
[html]
Workflows · Pipeline Troubleshooting Guide

Monitoring & Alerting

Core Concept
Understanding the difference between slow, stuck, and broken pipeline states is critical for effective troubleshooting. Each state has distinct indicators, root causes, and resolution strategies.
Section 01
Quick Reference — State Identification
State Identification
StateKey IndicatorsTypical Duration
SlowPipeline completes but takes 10× longer than baselineMinutes to hours
StuckStatus remains 'Running', 'Scheduled', or 'Preview' indefinitely with no progressHours to days
BrokenExplicit error messages: TimeoutError, Failed to fetch data, PusherBadRequestImmediate failure
Section 02
Slow Pipelines
Root Causes & Resolutions
  • Large datasets without materialization — each downstream node re-executes the full query chain. Resolution: enable Materialize on heavy nodes
  • Complex transformations — multiple joins, window functions, or recursive CTEs increase BigQuery execution time
  • Resource contention — multiple pipelines competing for CPU/memory in limited worker pod environments
Section 03
Stuck Pipelines
Root Causes & Resolutions
  • Calculation node misconfiguration — oversized function or improperly formatted logic hangs evaluation without throwing an error. Review and fix the Calculation node.
  • V1 pipeline deprecation — V1 pipelines appear scheduled but never execute. Migrate to Pipeline V2.
  • NATS messaging layer failure — stale connections cause pipelines to hang in scheduled state. Requires DevOps restart of NATS cluster.
  • Single-pod environments — during pod restarts, pipelines remain scheduled but cannot execute. Wait for pod to come back online.
  • BigQuery job callback failure — BigQuery completes but fails to send completion callback to Temporal. Short-term: retry the run.
Section 04
Broken Pipelines
Error Reference
Error TypeCauseResolution
temporalio.exceptions.TimeoutErrorTemporal activity stops sending heartbeat signals — node timeout, worker crash, or BigQuery hangRetry once; if recurring, break transformation into smaller steps; contact DevOps for Temporal worker health
Context Lostx-bluecopa-deployed-solution cookie cleared when navigating to Runs tabRefresh the page to restore the cookie — known UI bug being fixed
Worker Crash (OOMKilled)dfx-worker pod crashes during execution due to memory exhaustionCheck worker logs for OOMKilled events; DevOps may need to increase resource limits
PusherBadRequestNATS/messaging layer issueDevOps restart of NATS cluster
Section 05
Systematic Troubleshooting — 5 Steps
Diagnostic Sequence
  1. Check Pipeline Version — verify you're using Pipeline V2. V1 pipelines appear functional but won't execute.
  2. Inspect Node-Level Status — Loading/Buffering → Slow; No status change >30 min → Stuck; Red error indicator → Broken
  3. Review Execution Logs — TimeoutError → heartbeat timeout; PusherBadRequest → NATS issue; Failed to fetch data → BigQuery failure
  4. Check Environment Health — are other pipelines affected? (points to infrastructure-wide issue)
  5. Apply Resolution Strategy — Slow → optimize; Stuck → escalate or migrate; Broken → retry or debug
Section 06
When to Contact DevOps
Escalate Immediately If
  • Multiple pipelines across different workspaces failing simultaneously
  • Recurring TimeoutError on different nodes after retries
  • Pipelines stuck in 'Scheduled' state for >1 hour
  • Error messages mentioning NATS, Temporal, or worker pod names
Provide in Your Ticket
Pipeline ID and Run ID · Exact error message from logs · Approximate time of failure (with timezone) · Whether the issue affects one pipeline or multiple

articles.title: Error Handling & Retry Policy
articles.author: Sameera J
articles.content:
[html]
Workflows · Reliability Configuration

Error Handling & Retry Policy

Purpose
Defines how a workflow step handles timeouts, failures, and retry behaviour to ensure reliability and controlled execution under unstable conditions — preventing silent failures and ensuring downstream steps are managed correctly.
Section 01
Timeout Configuration

Timeout defines the maximum duration a workflow step is allowed to run before it is considered failed. If the step does not complete within the configured time, it is marked as a timeout error.

Timeout Settings
SettingDescription
Timeout (Seconds)Maximum allowed execution time for the step
Continue on Timeout: EnabledWorkflow continues to execute the next step if timeout occurs
Continue on Timeout: DisabledWorkflow fails immediately if timeout occurs
Section 02
Retry Policy
Retry Settings
SettingDescription
Interval (Seconds)Initial delay before the first retry attempt. System waits this duration after a failure, then retries.
Max AttemptsHow many times the system retries after failure. Once reached, no more retries — step is marked failed.
Backoff CoefficientMultiplier applied to the previous delay. Value of 2 doubles the delay each retry; 5 increases it 5× each time.
Continue on FailureWhether the workflow proceeds to the next step after all retries are exhausted. Useful for logging/cleanup steps that must run regardless.
Section 03
Example Configuration
Working Example
SettingValueEffect
Timeout5 secondsStep must complete within 5 seconds
Interval5 secondsWait 5 seconds before first retry
Max Attempts4Up to 4 retry attempts
Backoff Coefficient2.0Delays: 5s → 10s → 20s → 40s
Continue on TimeoutEnabledWorkflow proceeds even if timeout occurs
Continue on FailureDisabledWorkflow stops after all retries fail
Section 04
Retry Flow Walkthrough
Exponential Backoff
  1. Step fails → wait 5 seconds → retry attempt 1
  2. Fails again → wait 10 seconds (5 × 2) → retry attempt 2
  3. Fails again → wait 20 seconds (10 × 2) → retry attempt 3
  4. Fails again → wait 40 seconds (20 × 2) → retry attempt 4
  5. All retries exhausted → since Continue on Failure = Disabled → workflow stops
Section 05
Continue on Failure — Real-World Scenario

When Continue on Failure is enabled: the failed step is still marked as failed, but it does not block the remaining workflow. This is useful for scenarios where subsequent steps (logging, status updates, cleanup) must run regardless of earlier failures.

Example
Trigger step succeeds → Run Pipeline fails (all retries exhausted) → Because Continue on Failure = Enabled → Workflow proceeds → 'Updating input table with status' step executes successfully.

articles.title: API Integration Nodes
articles.author: Sai Kumar
articles.content:
[html]
Workflows · Implementation Guide

API Integration Nodes

What Is an API Integration Node?
A specialized workflow step embedded within a data pipeline or automation sequence. It acts as The Orchestrator — managing business data logic, mapping variables, and tracking transaction state records, before delegating low-level communication to the REST API Connector (the transport layer).
Section 01
Core Responsibilities
  • Business Logic Awareness — processes domain logic, handles conditional sequence logic, reads canvas parameters, and mutates workflow instance states based on data outcomes
  • Data Transformation & Contracting — validates mandatory field payloads, maps complex entities to external flat schemas, and prepares outbound data structures
  • State Machine & Exception Handling — tracks execution logs, evaluates response status codes, and routes to conditional branches, retry loops, or failure paths
  • Protocol Abstraction — completely agnostic to raw network sockets; relies entirely on the REST API Connector for transmission
Section 02
Runtime Lifecycle — Four Steps
Execution Sequence
  1. Map Dynamic Data Tokens — captures live variables from preceding workflow steps and maps them into API action template parameter placeholders
  2. Handle Context & Credential Verification — fetches active workspace tokens and identity metrics (e.g. x-bluecopa-workspace-id header) from the platform's secure secret state
  3. Execute Request Asynchronously — packages the payload and dispatches it to the network transporter, enforcing the configured socket timeout window
  4. Process Response Status Outcomes — monitors HTTP status codes to dictate subsequent workflow pathing
Section 03
HTTP Response Handling
Response Logic
Status CodeNode Behaviour
200 (Success)Parses response body (JSON), extracts key fields, updates tracking variables, passes to downstream actions
401 / 403Breaks thread execution, flags workflow as failed, signs a failure exception log, routes to failure path
429 / 5xxIntercepts transient failures, pauses execution, triggers exponential backoff retry loop before marking unrecoverable
Section 04
API Node vs REST Connector — Key Distinction
Architectural Distinction
DimensionAPI Integration NodeREST API Connector
LayerBusiness Process LayerInfrastructure Transport Layer
FocusDomain logic, data state, execution flowHTTP protocol, connection pooling, JSON serialization
Failure handlingRoutes to fallback branches, notifies teamsCaptures transient network drops and TCP errors
Retry logicActive — manages backoff loopAgnostic — simply processes what is passed to it
Configured inWorkflow CanvasExternal Data > Settings panel
Section 05
Concrete Example

An invoice creation event arrives containing an order record. The API Integration Node maps the order_id to the path, attaches required headers, the transport engine dispatches the request, and on success the node updates the tracking database.

// Incoming trigger payload
{
  "order_id": "ORD98765",
  "total_invoice_cost": 1099.50,
  "client_profile_id": "CUST-9823"
}

// Response on success
{
  "code": 200,
  "message": "Order retrieved successfully.",
  "details": {
    "order_id": "ORD98765",
    "status": "Delivered",
    "delivery_date": "2026-06-15"
  }
}

articles.title: Workflow Trigger Types
articles.author: Srikanth Ande
articles.content:
[html]
Workflows · Complete Guide

Workflow Trigger Types

What Is a Workflow Trigger?
The starting condition that causes a workflow to execute. Triggers fall into two families: Scheduled (time-based, fires at a pre-defined time) and Event-based (fires immediately when something specific happens — a data change, form submission, or file upload).
Section 01
All Nine Trigger Types
Trigger Reference
TriggerTypeWhen to Use
Dataset UpdateEvent-basedReact to data changes in real time — validations, notifications, sync
Form SubmissionEvent-basedProcessing service requests, intake forms, approval workflows
FileboxEvent-basedAuto-process incoming documents — invoices, contracts, reports
ScheduleScheduledNightly/weekly reports, periodic sync, digest emails, cleanup tasks
HTTP TriggerEvent-basedReceive webhooks from Stripe, GitHub, Slack, or any external system
Manual TriggerOn-demandTesting, ad-hoc operations, admin tasks requiring human decision
Process Task ReassignmentEvent-basedNotify new assignee, escalate reassigned tasks, log for compliance
External EventEvent-basedIoT sensors, Kafka/EventBridge streaming, partner system events
Workflow EventEvent-basedChain workflows together — broadcast results to multiple consumers
Section 02
Trigger Details
⚙ Dataset Update — Configuration Tips
Select the specific dataset and optionally filter by field conditions to avoid unnecessary runs. Distinguish between insert-only and insert-plus-update events.
⚙ Form Submission — Configuration Tips
Map form fields to clearly named variables at the trigger level. Add a confirmation step immediately after so submitters know their form was received.
⚙ Filebox — Configuration Tips
Configure allowed file types in filebox settings to prevent unexpected uploads. Add a virus check step early before processing any file content.
⚙ Schedule — Configuration Tips
Use a specific time such as 02:00 UTC to reduce peak-hour load. For runs under 5 minutes, consider whether an event-based trigger is more appropriate.
⚙ HTTP Trigger — Configuration Tips
Secure the endpoint with a shared secret or token validation step. Return a 200 response quickly and offload heavy processing to async steps.
⚙ Manual Trigger — Configuration Tips
Add an input form to collect parameters at run time. Restrict access with role-based permissions.
⚙ Workflow Event — Configuration Tips
Maintain a shared event catalogue across teams. Version event names (e.g. order.created.v2) to allow safe changes over time.
Section 03
Scheduled vs Event-Based — Choosing the Right Trigger
Comparison
DimensionScheduledEvent-Based
When it firesAt a fixed time or intervalImmediately when the condition is met
Best forReports, periodic sync, cleanupReal-time reactions to data or user actions
LatencyUp to the full schedule intervalNear-zero — fires within seconds
ComplexitySimple to configureRequires condition design and filtering

articles.title: Match & Exception Identification
articles.author: Bhavana Priya
articles.content:
[html]
Reconciliation · Complete Beginner's Guide

Match & Exception Identification

What Is Reconciliation?
The process of comparing two datasets and identifying matching records, non-matching records, missing transactions, duplicates, and balance differences — ensuring data accuracy and integrity across systems.
Section 01
Accessing the Module
Navigation
  1. Log in to your Bluecopa workspace
  2. From the left navigation menu, select Apps
  3. Click Reconciliation — you land on the Reconciliation Dashboard
Section 02
Reconciliation Types
Supported Types
TypeDescriptionExamples
Match Reconciliation (Line-by-Line)Compares individual transactions from two datasetsInvoice vs Payment, Sales Order vs Gateway Transaction
Balance ReconciliationCompares summarized balances to verify totals agreeGeneral Ledger vs Sub-Ledger, Trial Balance Validation
Section 03
Creating a New Reconciliation
Five Configuration Steps
  1. Basic Details — give a meaningful name and select type (Match or Balance)
  2. Dataset Selection — choose Primary Dataset (source of truth) and Secondary Dataset (source being verified)
  3. Define Matching Rules — configure rule groups that define how transactions are matched
  4. Configure Notifications — select recipients for run completion alerts
  5. Save and Execute — choose full refresh (Run All) or incremental (Run)
Section 04
Dataset Prerequisites
Before You Configure
RequirementDetail
Transaction-Level DataBoth datasets must contain individual transaction records — not aggregated summaries
Consistent Column NamesColumn names must be standardized — 'Amount' and 'amount' are treated differently
Matching Data TypesColumns used in match rules must have identical data types (Number ↔ Number, not Number ↔ Text)
Unique Key ValuesKey columns must contain unique values — duplicates cause incorrect matches
Section 05
Configuring Match Rules

Rules define how transactions should be matched. They are organized into Rule Groups where all conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.

How Rule Priority Works
Rules execute in priority order. Matched records are immediately removed from the pool and never re-evaluated by later rules. Rule Group 1 runs first across all records. Only unmatched records proceed to Group 2, then Group 3. This prevents duplicate matching and improves accuracy.
Section 06
Understanding Results
System-Generated Columns
System ColumnValuesMeaning
Copa Match GroupRule Group 1/2/3, Left Missing, Right MissingWhich rule matched it, or which side is missing a record
Copa Match StatusMatched / UnmatchedQuick pass/fail indicator
Copa Match TypeAuto Matched / Manual Matched / UnmatchedHow the match was made
Copa Match Count1 / 0Numeric flag — 1 has a match, 0 does not
Section 07
Manual Matching
How to Manually Match
  1. Select the unmatched transaction from the left dataset and its counterpart from the right dataset
  2. Click Match — Bluecopa creates a manual match between the two records
  3. The Copa Match Type column updates to Manual Matched for auditing purposes
Signal
A high volume of manual matches indicates your automatic rules may need refinement. Track this trend over time.
Section 08
Best Practices
  • Use unique identifiers as keys — transaction IDs, invoice numbers — never dates or amounts alone
  • Standardize column names before ingestion — resolve casing and naming inconsistencies
  • Verify data types match rule columns — type mismatches cause silent failures
  • Reserve Run All for configuration changes — use incremental Run for daily operations
  • Investigate Left Missing and Right Missing records after every run — they reveal upstream data issues
  • Monitor manual match volume over time — a rising trend signals a rule-quality problem

articles.title: Single-Level Approval Workflow
articles.author: Srinivas Puneeth
articles.content:
[html]
Approval Workflows · Beginner Guide

Single-Level Approval Workflow

Overview
An end-to-end approval workflow triggered when a requester submits the Approval Form. The workflow automates notifications, tracks the approval decision, and loops back for corrections if the request is rejected — until final approval is received.
Section 01
Key Components
Workflow Components
  • Approval Form — collects requester details and product/deal requirements
  • Hidden field element — controls visibility of the Deal Approver section per user role
  • Automated alerts and email notifications — sent at each stage transition
  • Task assignment — Deal Approver receives a TASK FOR APPROVAL with due date tracking
  • Repeat-Until loop — continues until the consent field equals APPROVED
Section 02
Business Use Case

Designed to automate the approval process for product, deal, or business requests submitted by users. The workflow routes requests to the designated approver, tracks decisions, sends notifications, and manages resubmissions when changes are required.

Section 03
Workflow Steps
Step-by-Step Process
StepWhat Happens
1Requester submits the Approval Form with Name, Designation/Role, Product Name, and Requirements
2Workflow creates a TASK FOR APPROVAL and assigns it to the Deal Approver
3Deal Approver reviews the request — APPROVED/REJECTED radio buttons and Remarks field are revealed via hidden field
4If APPROVED — confirmation notification sent, workflow completes
5If REJECTED — rejection notification sent to requester with comments, requester receives a task to revise and resubmit
6Repeat-Until loop continues until consent field equals APPROVED
Section 04
The Approval Form — Before & After
Form Visibility by Role
  • Requester view — Deal Approver section is hidden by the hidden_form_element. Only Name, Designation/Role, Product Name, and Requirements are visible
  • Approver view — Once the workflow assigns the approval task, the hidden field is toggled and the Deal Approver section becomes visible with APPROVED/REJECTED radio buttons and Remarks field
Section 05
Repeat-Until Loop
Loop Condition
The Repeat-Until node controls the loop that keeps reassigning the approval task until the correct consent is given. The loop exits only when the consent field equals APPROVED. Until then, the workflow reassigns the task and continues the cycle.
Section 06
Conclusion

The Single-Level Approval Workflow simplifies and automates the approval process through task assignments, notifications, and Repeat-Until logic. By reducing manual effort, improving visibility, and maintaining a clear approval trail, the workflow ensures a consistent, efficient, and transparent approval process.

articles.title: Escalation & SLA Handling
articles.author: Karthik Varma
articles.content:
[html]
Approval Workflows · Automated Escalation

Escalation & SLA Handling

The Problem This Solves
Every approval workflow has one fundamental risk: someone does not act in time. Escalation & SLA Handling ensures every task has a defined deadline, approvers are reminded automatically before it, and managers are notified automatically if it is missed — without any manual intervention.
Section 01
The Two-Layer Model

Bluecopa enforces SLAs through two independent layers on every Human Task node. They work together but do different things.

Two-Layer SLA Model
LayerConfigured ByWhat It DoesCan Approver Still Submit?
Soft DeadlineDue (In Hours)Sends in-app reminder alerts to the approver's Alerts tab inside BluecopaYes
Hard DeadlineTimeout (Seconds)Routes the workflow to the escalation branch. Escalation email fires. Task is timed out.No
Section 02
The Five Configuration Fields
Field Reference
FieldWhat It Controls
Due (In Hours)The SLA window — how long the approver has from task assignment
Due Alert Offset (In Hours)How many hours before Due the first reminder fires
Due Alert Interval (In Minutes)How often the reminder repeats after the first alert
Timeout (Seconds)The hard cutoff — when this hits zero, the escalation branch fires
Continue on TimeoutMust be UNCHECKED — if checked, escalation never fires
Important
Due (In Hours) and Timeout (Seconds) are independent. You can set Due = 48 hours and Timeout = 86400 seconds (24 hours). The alerts start at hour 44 but the hard escalation fires at hour 24. Set them to match your business need.
Section 03
Example — Vendor Onboarding Workflow

A vendor onboarding workflow with three sequential approval stages, each with its own SLA clock, reminder schedule, and escalation path.

Approval Chain
StageApproverSLAEscalates To
1Legal Team48 hrsLegal Head / AP Manager
2Finance Team24 hrsFinance Manager
3Junior Finance24 hrsAP Head / Senior Finance
Section 04
SLA Configuration Per Stage
Configuration Values
FieldLegal Team (48h)Finance Team (24h)Junior Finance (24h)
Due (In Hours)482424
Due Alert Offset (In Hours)442
Due Alert Interval (In Minutes)606030
Timeout (Seconds)1728008640086400
Continue on TimeoutUncheckedUncheckedUnchecked
Section 05
Setting Up Email Escalation
Email Escalation Setup
  1. From the Human Task node, pull a connection from the timeout output handle to a Send Email node
  2. Set Type = Action, Action Type = Send Email
  3. Enter the manager's email in the Recipient field
  4. Write a clear subject: Action Required — [Stage] Review Overdue
  5. In the body, use dynamic variables: vendor name, due date, assignee name, process ID
  6. Set Max Attempts = 3, Backoff Coefficient = 2 for reliable retry on failure
Section 06
Post-Approval Actions
After Full Approval
  • INSERT to master list — RUN_INPUT_TABLE_ACTION writes the complete vendor record to the master input table, triggering downstream QB/Xero sync
  • Welcome email to vendor — fires automatically if Finance Team set Vendor Portal Access Required = Yes during their review

articles.title: Approval via Email
articles.author: Dharma Teja Taddi
articles.content:
[html]
Approval Workflows · Human-in-the-Loop

Approval via Email

What is Approval via Email?
A secure capability in Bluecopa that lets approvers act on pending tasks directly from their inbox — no password required. When a workflow reaches an approval checkpoint, Bluecopa sends a notification email with a unique action link. The approver clicks it, receives an OTP to the same inbox, enters it, and lands directly on the task.
Section 01
The Six-Stage Flow
Approver Journey
  1. Notification email received — personalised greeting, task summary, and a prominent action button (e.g. Review & Submit)
  2. Approver clicks the action button — Bluecopa validates the link, identifies the approver, generates a fresh OTP, and redirects to the OTP screen
  3. OTP entry — approver copies the code from their inbox and enters it on the Bluecopa login screen
  4. Authentication & redirect — once OTP is verified, the approver is automatically redirected to the task interface
  5. Task completion — approver reviews the full record, uploads documents, fills fields, and submits
  6. Workflow advances — decision is recorded with timestamp, task is marked complete, downstream automation triggers immediately
Section 02
OTP & Session Behaviour
Important Rules
ScenarioBehaviour
OTP generated but approver does not log inOTP does not expire — valid until used or task expires
Approver logs in but does not submitSession expires after the configured task expiry period. New delegated task required.
Approver logs in and submitsAction link expires permanently. No manual cleanup needed.
Section 03
Required Workflow Nodes
Three-Node Configuration
  • Node 1 — Create Delegated Task — creates the task record with expiry and fault-tolerance settings
  • Node 2 — Send Notification Email — dispatches the action link email to the approver
  • Node 3 — Log to Tracking Table (Recommended) — creates an auditable record for compliance and follow-up
Section 04
Best Practices
Configuration Checklist
  • Use a clear, action-oriented subject line — e.g. Action Required: [Task Name]
  • Label the CTA button with the action — e.g. Review & Submit rather than just Click Here
  • Inform approvers in advance that they will receive two emails: the action link and the OTP
  • Advise approvers never to forward either email — both are personal and single-use
  • Set a realistic expiry window — 7 days works well for most approval cycles
  • Never reuse a delegated task ID — always generate a new task per batch
  • End-to-end test with a single approver before batch activation

articles.title: Conditional Routing Workflow — Different Paths Based on Approve vs Reject
articles.author: Pradyumn Vibhandik
articles.excerpt: A step-by-step breakdown of the Conditional Routing workflow that automates document classification and routing into Fileboxes based on approver selection — covering form configuration, pipeline nodes, conditional logic, and troubleshooting.
articles.content:
[html]
Implementation Story · Unique Scenario
Conditional Routing Workflow
Different Paths Based on Approve vs Reject
Form Trigger Approver Task Conditional Routing Drop To Filebox
Section 1
Overview
How the Conditional Routing workflow automates document classification and storage

The Conditional Routing workflow automates the classification and routing of uploaded documents into the appropriate repository based on the approver's selection. It eliminates manual sorting by guiding each document through a structured pipeline — from upload to final storage.

Key Components
Form Trigger
Initiates the workflow when a document is uploaded by the user.
Form Update Activity
Updates the hidden field to reveal the Selection Panel to the approver.
Approver Task
Allows the approver to preview and classify the uploaded document.
Selection Panel
Provides four document classification options: Invoice, PO, DC, or Reject.
Conditional Routing
Evaluates the selected document type and determines the routing path.
Drop To Filebox
Moves the file to the designated Filebox repository based on document type.
Section 2
Business Use Case
Why this workflow exists and what business problem it solves

Organisations receive multiple document types — Invoices, Purchase Orders, and Delivery Challans — through a single intake channel. Manually reviewing and sorting these into the correct repositories is time-consuming and error-prone. This workflow streamlines the process: the approver classifies the document and the system automatically routes it to the correct Filebox — no manual file movement required.

Business Benefits
  • ✓ Automated document classification — removes the need for manual sorting.
  • ✓ Reduced manual effort — approver only needs to select the document type.
  • ✓ Improved document organisation — each document lands in the correct Filebox.
  • ✓ Faster processing — routing happens instantly after the approver submits.
  • ✓ Consistent routing — same logic applied every time, no human error.
  • ✓ Easy scalability — new document types can be added by extending the routing conditions.
Section 3
Form Configuration
The three key form elements and how they work together

The workflow begins with a form that the user interacts with to upload a document. The form contains three key elements: the File Drop control, a hidden form element that controls visibility, and a Selection Panel that becomes visible only to the approver after the pipeline processes the submission.

3.1 — User View · Upload Screen

When the user opens the form, they see a clean file upload interface. The Selection Panel is intentionally hidden at this stage — the user's only action is to upload a document and submit the form.

3.2 — Form Designer View · Full Configuration

In the form designer, all three elements are visible: the File Drop control at the top, the hidden_form_element below it, and the Selection Panel at the bottom. The Selection Panel is configured to appear only when the hidden field value equals A2 — which only happens after the Form Update Activity runs in the workflow pipeline.

3.3 — Control Properties
📎 File Drop Control
Namefile_form
PlaceholderDrag and drop or click to upload file
Enable Preview✅ Enabled — allows approver to preview the document in-task
🔒 Hidden Form Element
Namehidden_form_element
Default ValueA1 — Selection Panel stays hidden
After pipelineUpdated to A2 — Selection Panel becomes visible
☰ Selection Panel
Nameradio_form
OptionsInvoice · Purchase Order · Delivery Challan · Reject
Required✅ Checked
Visible whenhidden_form_element = A2
Section 4
Workflow Pipeline
How the pipeline runs once the user submits the form

Once the user submits the form, the workflow pipeline activates automatically. The pipeline runs a sequence of activities that update the form state and assign the task to the approver — without any further input from the user.

4.2 — How Each Node Works
Node What It Does
Trigger (Form) Entry point. Fires automatically the moment the user submits the form with the uploaded document. No manual action needed.
activity_1_ (Form Update) Updates hidden_form_element from A1 → A2, unlocking the Selection Panel visibility condition.
TASK APPROVER Creates and assigns the review task. The approver opens the task, previews the document, and selects the document type from the now-visible Selection Panel. Pipeline pauses here until approver submits.
Condition Nodes
Invoice / PO / DC / Reject		 Four condition nodes evaluate the approver's selection in sequence (INV → PO → DC → REJ). Each checks whether the Selection Panel value matches. If Yes, the Drop To Filebox activity runs. If No, moves to the next condition.
Drop To Filebox
inv / po / dc / rej		 Final action node. Physically moves the uploaded file into its destination Filebox. Only the matched condition's node executes — the others are skipped. Workflow completes after this.
4.3 — All Four Drop To Filebox Nodes
Node Name Condition Value Destination Filebox
inv INV Invoice Filebox
po PO PO Filebox
dc DC Delivery Challan Filebox
rej REJ Rejected Documents Filebox
Section 5
Step-by-Step Process
Every step from document upload to final routing
# Activity Description
1 Form Submission User opens the form and uploads a document using the File Drop control.
2 Form Update Activity Pipeline triggers automatically. The hidden_form_element value is updated from A1 to A2.
3 Selection Panel Revealed The Selection Panel becomes visible to the approver as the visibility condition is now met.
4 Approver Task Assigned The uploaded document is assigned to the approver as a task for review.
5 Document Review The approver opens the task, previews the document, and identifies the document type.
6 Document Type Selection The approver selects one option from the Selection Panel: Invoice, Purchase Order, Delivery Challan, or Reject.
7 Conditional Routing Evaluated The workflow checks the selected value against defined conditions (INV, PO, DC, REJ) in sequence.
8 File Routing Based on the matched condition, the document is automatically moved to the corresponding Filebox.
9 Workflow Complete The process ends successfully with the document stored in the correct repository.
Section 6
Approver Review — Document Classification
What the approver sees and does in their task screen

Once the task is assigned, the approver receives a notification and opens the task. The approver's screen shows the uploaded document alongside the Selection Panel. The approver must preview the document, identify its type, and select the appropriate option before submitting.

👁️
Preview Document
Opens the task, uses the Preview tab to view the uploaded document inline — no download required.
☑️
Select Document Type
Identifies the document and selects the matching option: Invoice, PO, Delivery Challan, or Reject.
🚀
Submit Task
Clicking Submit triggers conditional routing — the matched condition activates Drop To Filebox instantly.
Section 7
Conditional Routing Logic
How each selection maps to an action and destination

After the approver submits the task, the workflow evaluates the selected value using a sequence of conditional checks. Each condition is checked in order — Invoice first, then Purchase Order, then Delivery Challan, then Reject. When a condition matches, the corresponding Drop To Filebox activity runs.

Selection Condition Code Action Destination Filebox
Invoice INV Drop To Filebox Invoice Filebox
Purchase Order PO Drop To Filebox PO Filebox
Delivery Challan DC Drop To Filebox Delivery Challan Filebox
Reject REJ Drop To Filebox Rejected Documents Filebox
Section 8
End-to-End Flow
Complete journey from document upload to final storage
📤 Document Upload
User submits form

↓
👤 Task Assigned to Approver
↓

↓
☑️ Approver Selects Document Type
↓
🔀 Conditional Routing Evaluated
INV / PO / DC / REJ
↓
📁 Invoice
Filebox

Section 9
Troubleshooting
Common issues and how to resolve them
Issue Resolution
Selection Panel Not Visible Verify hidden_form_element is updated from A1 to A2 by the Form Update Activity.
File Not Routed Verify the approver's selection matches exactly: INV, PO, DC, or REJ.
File Missing in Filebox Validate the Filebox configuration and ensure the correct Filebox is mapped in the Drop To Filebox node.
Workflow Stops Unexpectedly Verify the conditional routing configuration and check all condition branches are set correctly.
Section 10
Conclusion

The Conditional Routing workflow provides a reliable, automated solution for document classification and storage. By combining a user-facing upload form, a pipeline-driven form update, an approver review task, and conditional routing logic, the workflow ensures that every document is reviewed and stored in the correct Filebox — consistently and without manual intervention.

The design intentionally separates the user's experience (simple upload) from the approver's experience (review and classify), using the hidden_form_element as a state flag that bridges the two. This approach keeps the user interface clean while giving the approver all the tools needed to make an accurate classification.

articles.content:
## Overview

This is a complete reference of all menu items across the Bluecopa platform. Each section describes what the menu does and when a user would navigate there.

---

## Top-Level Navigation (Navbar)

These are the primary icons in the left navbar, always visible.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Home** | `/home` | The landing page after login. Shows a personalised view of favourited dashboards, statements, and metrics. Users pin their most-used assets here for quick access instead of navigating through the full menu each time. |
| **Inbox** | `/inbox/alerts` | Central hub for all notifications and tasks. System-generated alerts (e.g., pipeline failures, data refresh completions) appear here alongside manually assigned tasks. Think of it as the user's to-do list and notification centre combined. |
| **Workspace** | `/workspace` | Overview of the current workspace. A workspace is a tenant-level container — all data, users, and configurations are scoped to it. This page shows workspace-level activity and recent items. |
| **Solutions** | `/solutions` | Manage packaged solutions that bundle workbooks, dashboards, and pipelines into deployable units. Solutions support branching (like git) so teams can develop changes in isolation and publish them to production. Used heavily for client-facing deliverables. |
| **Operations** | `/operations/databox` | Day-to-day operational hub for data processing. This is where operations teams upload data, trigger workflows, monitor running jobs, and download outputs. Designed for recurring, production-grade data work rather than one-off analysis. |
| **Library** | `/library/catalog/dashboard?page=1` | The published asset catalogue — a read-only storefront of all shared dashboards, statements, metrics, datasets, and portals. When analysts finish building something in the workspace, they publish it to the Library for others to discover and consume. |

---

## Accounting Studio

The accounting-focused module suite. Groups together reconciliation, cost allocation, and ledger management — the core workflows for finance and accounting teams.

### Reconciliation Engine

Automates the process of matching and reconciling data across systems (e.g., bank statements vs. GL entries). Finance teams use this to ensure numbers agree across sources and flag discrepancies.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Reconciliations** | `/reconciliation-engine/reconciliations` | Configuration hub for reconciliation rules. Users define matching criteria (exact match, fuzzy match, tolerance-based), map source columns, and set up multi-step reconciliation flows. Each config represents a repeatable reconciliation process that can be scheduled or triggered manually. |
| **Data** | `/reconciliation-engine/data` | View the output of reconciliation runs. Shows matched records, unmatched exceptions, and summary statistics. This is where users investigate why certain records didn't match and take corrective action (adjust, write off, or escalate). |

### Allocation Engine

Handles cost and revenue allocation — distributing amounts from one set of accounts/entities to another based on configurable rules. Used by FP&A and accounting teams for overhead allocation, transfer pricing, and profitability analysis.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Methods** | `/allocations/blueprints` | Define reusable allocation logic as "methods" (internally called blueprints). Each method specifies how to distribute costs — e.g., allocate IT overhead proportionally by headcount, or split shared services by revenue percentage. Methods are building blocks that get assembled into pipelines. |
| **Templated Data** | `/allocations/data-preparation` | Prepare and transform source data into the structured format that allocation methods expect. Templated data acts as a mapping layer — users define how raw data columns map to the inputs required by their methods. This ensures data consistency across different allocation runs. |
| **Pipelines** | `/allocations/workflows` | Orchestrate end-to-end allocation runs by chaining methods, data preparation steps, and output destinations into executable pipelines. A pipeline defines the full sequence: load data → apply method A → apply method B → write results. Users can run pipelines manually or schedule them. |
| **Allocation Schedules** | `/allocations/allocation-schedules` | Schedule allocation pipelines to run automatically on defined cadences (daily, weekly, monthly). Shows run history with status (success/failure), execution time, and logs. Used for recurring month-end or quarter-end allocation processes that need to run reliably without manual intervention. |
| **Allocation P&L** | `/allocations/profit-and-loss` | Profit and loss analysis view built from allocation results. Shows how costs and revenues flow through the allocation hierarchy — users can drill down from summary totals to individual allocation line items. Includes scenario comparison to see how different allocation methods affect the bottom line. |
| **Page Templates** | `/allocations/page-templates` | Reusable page layouts for allocation reports. Templates define the visual structure (tables, charts, KPIs) so that when new allocation results come in, they automatically populate into a consistent report format. Saves time when producing standardised allocation reports for stakeholders. |

### Period Close (Ledger Management)

Manages journal entries and ledger data for period-close processes. Used by accounting teams to post adjustments, accruals, and reclassifications during month-end or year-end close.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Ledger Entries** | `/period-close/ledgers` | Create, review, and manage journal entries. Users can post manual adjustments, import bulk entries, and track the approval status of each entry. Entries are organised by period and ledger, making it easy to see all postings for a given close cycle. |
| **Data** | `/period-close/data` | View the consolidated results of ledger postings. Shows trial balances, period comparisons, and entry details. This is the "after" view — once entries are posted, users come here to verify that balances are correct before closing the period. |

---

## Apps Studio

The low-code application builder. Users create data-driven apps (tables, portals, robots, workflows) without writing code. Think of it as the platform's internal app development environment.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Tables** | `/apps-studio/input-table` | Spreadsheet-like data entry tables. Users define schemas (columns, types, validations) and then enter or import data. Tables are the primary way to get manual/human-entered data into the platform — e.g., budget inputs, adjustment entries, or reference mappings. |
| **View Tables** | `/apps-studio/view-table` | Read-only table views over existing datasets. Unlike input tables, these don't allow editing — they surface data from other sources (databases, APIs) in a tabular format for review. Useful for giving stakeholders visibility without edit access. |
| **Portals** | `/apps-studio/portals` | Interactive data applications built from components (tables, charts, forms, filters). Portals are published to the Library and shared with end users. Think of them as lightweight dashboards with input capabilities — users can both view data and submit changes. |
| **Custom Portals** | `/apps-studio/custom-portals` | Advanced portal builder for more complex layouts and custom logic. Supports richer interactions than standard portals — custom JavaScript, conditional rendering, and multi-step forms. Used when standard portal components aren't enough. |
| **SkillSets** | `/apps-studio/skillsets` | AI copilot builder. Users define "skills" that teach the AI assistant how to answer domain-specific questions using the platform's data. Each SkillSet connects to datasets and defines the context the AI needs to provide accurate, grounded responses. |
| **Blob Connections** | `/apps-studio/blob-connections` | Connect to cloud blob storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS). Once connected, users can browse, upload, and manage files directly from the platform. Used for ingesting unstructured data (PDFs, images, CSVs) or storing generated outputs. |
| **External Apps** | `/apps-studio/ext-apps` | Register and manage external micro-frontend applications that embed into the platform. External apps run in isolation (single-spa) but share authentication and navigation. Used for extending the platform with custom-built UIs. |
| **Tables V2** | `/apps/input-table-v2` | Next-generation input tables with schema migration support. Unlike v1, Tables V2 tracks schema changes over time (add/remove/rename columns) and applies migrations automatically. Opens in a separate app (external link). |
| **Robots** | `/apps-studio/robots` | Configure automated bots that perform repetitive tasks. Robots can be triggered on schedule or by events — e.g., "when a new file lands in Filebox, parse it and load into Table X." They combine actions (API calls, data transforms, notifications) into reusable automations. |
| **Workflows** | `/apps-studio/processes` | Visual workflow builder for multi-step business processes. Define sequences of tasks with approvals, conditions, and parallel branches. Workflows coordinate human and automated steps — e.g., "data analyst uploads → manager approves → system processes → finance reviews." |
| **Workflow Events** | `/apps-studio/workflow-events` | Define and manage events that trigger workflows. Events can be time-based (cron), data-driven (new record inserted), or external (webhook received). This is the "when" configuration — what conditions cause a workflow to start executing. |

---

## Data Studio

The data engineering and transformation hub. Combines allocation engine tools (for cost allocation pipelines) with data cleaning, dbt integration, and legacy pipeline management. This is where data teams build and manage their transformation layer.

| Menu Item | Route | Source | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Methods** | `/data-studio/methods` | Allocation Engine | Allocation methods (blueprints) — same as Allocation Engine but accessed from the Data Studio context. The sidebar stays as Data Studio when navigating here, keeping the data engineering workflow uninterrupted. |
| **Templated Data** | `/data-studio/templated-data` | Allocation Engine | Data preparation and mapping templates — same functionality as the Allocation Engine version. Accessible here so data engineers don't need to switch to the accounting module to set up data mappings. |
| **Pipelines** | `/data-studio/allocation-workflows` | Allocation Engine | Allocation pipeline orchestration — same as Allocation Engine pipelines. Available here because data teams often build and maintain these pipelines alongside their other data transformation work. |
| **Allocation Schedules** | `/data-studio/allocation-schedules` | Allocation Engine | Schedule management for allocation pipelines — same as the Allocation Engine version. Included here so data ops teams can manage all their scheduled jobs from one place. |
| **Clean** | `/data-studio/datasets?type=transaction` | Native | Data quality tools for identifying and resolving duplicates, invalid entries, and inconsistencies in transaction datasets. Users upload or connect raw data, run cleaning rules, and review flagged records before promoting clean data downstream. |
| **Dbt Pipelines** | `/data-studio/dbt-pipelines` | Native | Integration with dbt (data build tool) for SQL-based data transformations. Users connect their dbt projects, configure environment variables, trigger builds, and monitor job status. This is the primary transformation tool for teams using the modern dbt workflow. |
| **Pipelines (Deprecated)** | `/data-studio/pipelines` | Native | The original visual pipeline builder for data transformations. Allows drag-and-drop construction of data flows (extract → transform → load). Marked as deprecated because dbt pipelines and allocation workflows now cover these use cases with better tooling and maintainability. |
| **Exports** | `/data-studio/bulk-exports` | Native | Download centre for bulk data exports. When users trigger large exports (e.g., full dataset downloads, report generation), the jobs run asynchronously and the finished files appear here for download. Shows export history, file sizes, and expiration dates. |

---

## Integrations

Connect the platform to external systems. This is the central place to manage all inbound and outbound data connections — files, databases, APIs, email, and event streams.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Files** | `/integrations/connections/connected?type=FILE` | File-based data connections. Connect to file sources (SFTP, cloud storage, local upload) to ingest CSV, Excel, JSON, and other file formats. Each connection defines the source location, file format, and parsing rules. Used for recurring file-based data feeds. |
| **Apps** | `/integrations/connections/connected?type=APP` | Application integrations (Salesforce, HubSpot, QuickBooks, etc.). Pre-built connectors that authenticate with third-party apps and sync data on schedule. Users map external app objects/fields to platform datasets for automated data ingestion. |
| **Databases** | `/integrations/connections/connected?type=DB` | Direct database connections (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Snowflake, etc.). Users provide connection credentials and can query external databases directly or set up scheduled data pulls. Supports both read (ingestion) and write (export) operations. |
| **External Datasets** | `/integrations/external-datasets` | Datasets that live in external systems but are queryable from the platform. Unlike regular connections that copy data in, external datasets query the source on demand. Useful for large datasets where full replication isn't practical. |
| **External Data** | `/integrations/external-connections` | Generic external data connections for systems that don't fit the file/app/database categories. Covers REST APIs, custom protocols, and specialised data sources. Users configure endpoints, authentication, and data mapping manually. |
| **HTTP Triggers** | `/integrations/http-triggers` | Webhook endpoints that external systems can call to push data into the platform or trigger workflows. Each trigger generates a unique URL — when an external system POSTs to it, the platform processes the payload and routes it to the configured destination. |
| **Email Connections** | `/integrations/email-connections` | Configure email-based data ingestion and notification. Inbound: parse data from email attachments automatically. Outbound: send reports, alerts, and exports via email. Each connection defines the mail server, credentials, and processing rules. |
| **SFTP Connections** | `/integrations/sftp-connections` | Connect to SFTP servers for secure file transfer. Used for automated file exchange with partners, banks, and legacy systems that require SFTP. Supports scheduled uploads/downloads and file monitoring (trigger workflow when new file arrives). |
| **Workflow Logs** | `/data/workflow-logs` | Centralised log viewer for all workflow executions across the platform. Shows execution history, step-by-step details, errors, and timing. Essential for debugging failed integrations and monitoring data pipeline health. |
| **External Events** | `/integrations/pub-sub` | Pub/sub event streaming connections. Subscribe to external event streams (Kafka, AWS SNS/SQS, etc.) or publish events from the platform. Used for real-time data integration where batch/scheduled approaches are too slow. |

---

## Inbox

The notification and task management centre. Aggregates system alerts, user-assigned tasks, and configuration for what triggers notifications.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Alerts** | `/inbox/alerts` | Real-time feed of system events — pipeline completions, failures, data quality warnings, approval requests, and scheduled job results. Each alert links to the relevant asset so users can take action immediately. Alerts are generated automatically based on system activity. |
| **My Tasks** | `/inbox/tasks` | Personal task list showing all tasks assigned to the current user. Tasks can be system-generated (e.g., "review this reconciliation exception") or manually assigned by other users. Includes due dates, priority, and status tracking. |
| **Notifications** | `/inbox/settings` | Configure notification preferences — which events trigger notifications, delivery channel (in-app, email, or both), and frequency (instant, daily digest). Users can suppress noisy alerts or escalate critical ones to email. |
| **Alert Configurations** | `/inbox/alert-configs` | Define custom alert rules beyond the system defaults. Users specify conditions (e.g., "if pipeline X fails more than 3 times in 24 hours") and actions (notify team, create task, trigger workflow). This is the rule engine behind the alerts system. |

---

## Operations

The production operations hub for day-to-day data work. While other sections focus on building and configuring, Operations is where the actual data flows happen — upload, process, monitor, download.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Databox** | `/operations/databox` | Structured data inbox. External and internal data arrives here in defined schemas — think of it as a staging area where data lands before being processed. Users can review incoming data, trigger processing workflows, and track the status of each data package through its lifecycle. |
| **Filebox** | `/operations/filebox` | Unstructured file storage. Unlike Databox (which expects structured data), Filebox accepts any file type — PDFs, images, spreadsheets, documents. Files can be tagged, organised into folders, and attached to workflows for processing. Used when data arrives in non-tabular formats. |
| **My Workflows** | `/operations/processes` | Personal view of workflow instances the user is involved in. Shows active workflows, pending approvals, and completed processes. Unlike the Apps Studio workflow builder (which defines templates), this shows running instances — the actual work in progress. |
| **Downloads** | `/operations/bulk-exports` | Download centre for completed export jobs. When large data exports are triggered (from datasets, reports, or portals), they process asynchronously and appear here when ready. Files are available for a limited time before expiring. |
| **Monitors** | `/operations/monitors` | Real-time monitoring dashboard for all running processes — data ingestions, transformations, allocations, and scheduled jobs. Shows status, progress, duration, and resource usage. Operations teams use this as their primary "control room" to ensure everything is running smoothly. |
| **Delegated Tasks** | `/operations/delegated-tasks` | Manage tasks that have been delegated to or from the current user. When a user is unavailable (vacation, role change), their tasks can be delegated to a colleague. This view shows the delegation chain so nothing falls through the cracks. |

---

## Library

The published asset catalogue. Everything built in the platform (dashboards, datasets, portals) can be published to the Library for organisation-wide consumption. The Library is read-only for consumers — editing happens in the Workspace.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Dashboards** | `/library/catalog/dashboard?page=1` | Browse published dashboards. Dashboards combine charts, tables, and KPIs into interactive visual pages. Published dashboards are versioned — updates go through a publish cycle so consumers always see a stable, validated version. |
| **Statements** | `/library/catalog/statement?page=1` | Browse published financial statements. Statements are structured tabular reports (income statements, balance sheets, custom reports) with drill-down capabilities. They pull from live data but present it in a fixed, auditable format. |
| **Metrics** | `/library/catalog/pivot?page=1` | Browse published metrics (pivot tables). Metrics are pre-configured analytical views that users can slice and dice by dimensions. Published metrics ensure everyone in the organisation uses the same calculation logic and data source. |
| **Datasets** | `/library/catalog/datasets?page=1` | Browse published datasets. Published datasets are curated, validated data tables that serve as the "single source of truth" for downstream analysis. They include documentation, lineage, and access controls. |
| **Virtual Datasets** | `/library/virtual-datasets?page=1` | Browse published virtual datasets. Unlike regular datasets (which store data), virtual datasets are query definitions that compute results on the fly. They're lightweight pointers to underlying data with transformations applied at read time. |
| **System Tables** | `/library/system-table?page=1` | Browse system-managed reference tables. These are platform-maintained tables (e.g., currency codes, country lists, calendar hierarchies) that are available to all workspaces. Users can reference them in formulas and joins but cannot modify them. |
| **Templated Data** | `/library/templated-data` | Browse published templated data (allocation mappings). When allocation data templates are finalised and validated, they're published here for reuse across different allocation methods and pipelines. |
| **Portals** | `/library/portals` | Browse published portals. Portals are interactive data apps (built in Apps Studio) that combine data display with user input. Published portals are accessible to end users who need to both view reports and submit data. |
| **Data Access** | `/library/data-access` | Manage who can access which published datasets. Defines row-level and column-level security rules — e.g., "regional managers can only see data for their region." This is the authorisation layer that controls data visibility across the organisation. |
| **Assemblies** | `/library/assemblies` | Compose solution assemblies — bundles of related assets (dashboards, datasets, portals) packaged together for deployment. Assemblies make it easy to ship a complete solution (e.g., "Monthly Close Package") as a single unit rather than managing individual assets. |

---

## Settings

Platform configuration — user preferences, workspace-wide settings, access control, and security.

### Access & Security

Manage who has access to what. User and team management, audit trails, and credential storage.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Users** | `/settings/users` | Manage platform users — invite new users, assign roles (Admin, Editor, Viewer), activate/deactivate accounts, and configure per-user permissions. Each user belongs to a workspace and can be added to teams for group-based access control. |
| **Teams** | `/settings/teams` | Create and manage teams — logical groups of users for bulk permission assignment. Instead of granting access to individual users, admins assign permissions to teams. When a user joins a team, they inherit all the team's access rights automatically. |
| **Audit** | `/audit` | View the complete audit trail of all actions taken in the workspace. Every data modification, login, permission change, and configuration update is logged with timestamp, user, and details. Required for compliance (SOX, SOC2) and useful for investigating unexpected changes. |
| **Credentials** | `/settings/credentials` | Manage stored credentials for external system connections (database passwords, API keys, OAuth tokens). Credentials are encrypted at rest and referenced by name in integrations — so connection configs don't contain plaintext secrets. Supports rotation and expiry tracking. |
| **Secrets** | `/settings/secrets` | Key-value secret store for sensitive configuration values (API tokens, encryption keys, service accounts). Similar to credentials but more general-purpose — secrets can be referenced in workflows, robots, and custom code without exposing the actual values in configuration. |

### User Preferences

Personal settings that affect only the current user's experience.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Number** | `/settings/number` | Configure how numbers are displayed for the current user — decimal separator (comma vs. period), thousands grouping, negative number format, and default decimal places. These preferences override workspace defaults and apply across all views. |
| **Theme** | `/settings/theme` | Customise the visual appearance — colour scheme, font size, and display density. Theme changes are applied immediately and persist across sessions. Useful for accessibility needs or personal preference. |

### Workspace Settings

Organisation-wide configuration that applies to all users in the workspace.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Currency** | `/settings/workspace/currency` | Define the workspace's base currency and configure exchange rate sources. All monetary values in the platform are stored and displayed relative to this base currency. Supports multi-currency workspaces with automatic conversion using configured rates. |
| **Number** | `/settings/workspace/number` | Set the default number formatting for the entire workspace — decimal places, separators, and display conventions. Individual users can override these in their personal settings, but this defines the organisational standard. |
| **Calendar** | `/settings/workspace/calendar` | Configure the fiscal calendar — fiscal year start month, period structure (monthly, 4-4-5, custom), and period naming. This is critical for financial reporting because it defines what "Q1" and "Year-End" mean for the organisation. All date-based aggregations use this calendar. |
| **Labels** | `/settings/workspace/labels` | Manage workspace-wide tags/labels that can be applied to any asset (workbooks, pipelines, datasets). Labels enable filtering and organisation across the platform — e.g., "Production," "Draft," "Q4-Close." Defined once here, available everywhere. |
| **Theme** | `/settings/workspace/theme` | Set the default visual theme for the entire workspace — branding colours, logo, and default appearance. Unlike personal theme settings, this affects the default experience for all users and is typically configured to match corporate branding. |
| **Email Send** | `/settings/workspace/email-notification` | Configure the outbound email system — SMTP server, sender address, email templates, and delivery rules. Controls how the platform sends notification emails, report deliveries, and alert messages to users and external recipients. |
| **Docker Templates** | `/settings/workspace/docker-templates` | Manage Docker container templates for custom code execution. When users need to run custom Python/R/SQL scripts as part of workflows, the platform spins up containers from these templates. Admins configure base images, resource limits, and pre-installed packages. |
| **AI Settings** | `/settings/workspace/ai-settings` | Configure AI/copilot behaviour for the workspace — model selection, token limits, data access scope, and safety guardrails. Controls which datasets the AI can access when answering questions and how it generates responses. |
| **General** | `/settings/workspace/general` | General workspace configuration — workspace name, timezone, default language, and feature flags. Also includes data retention policies, session timeout settings, and other platform-wide behaviours that don't fit into more specific categories. |
| **Approvals** | `/settings/workspace/approvals` | Configure approval workflows — define who can approve what (data changes, publishing, user access), approval chains (single approver, multi-level), and escalation rules. Approvals add governance to critical actions so nothing goes to production without proper sign-off. |
| **Policies** | `/settings/workspace/policies` | Define conditional approval policies using rules. Unlike static approvals (which always require the same approvers), policies evaluate conditions at runtime — e.g., "if the amount exceeds $100K, require VP approval; otherwise, manager approval is sufficient." Built on the policy engine. |

### System Info

Platform information and device management.

| Menu Item | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Devices** | `/settings/devices` | View and manage devices that have accessed the user's account. Shows login history by device (browser, OS, IP address), active sessions, and allows revoking access from specific devices. Useful for security monitoring — spot unauthorised access or clean up stale sessions. |
| **About** | `/settings/about` | Platform version information, build details, and environment configuration. Shows the current release version, API endpoints, and system health status. Useful for support tickets and debugging — "which version are you running?" is answered here. |

---

## Key Takeaways

- The left navbar provides access to seven top-level areas: Home, Inbox, Workspace, Solutions, Operations, Library, and Accounting Studio.
- Accounting Studio groups the three core finance workflows — Reconciliation Engine, Allocation Engine, and Period Close (Ledger Management) — into one module suite for finance teams.
- Apps Studio is the low-code builder for data-driven applications including input tables, portals, robots, workflows, and AI SkillSets.
- Data Studio is the engineering hub for data transformations, supporting dbt pipelines, data cleaning, allocation workflows, and bulk exports.
- The Library is the published asset catalogue (read-only for consumers) where dashboards, statements, metrics, datasets, and portals are shared organisation-wide.
- Settings covers access control (Users, Teams, Audit, Credentials), user preferences (Theme, Number format), workspace configuration (Calendar, Currency, Approvals, Policies), and system information.
